段佑霖

Brief Overview of Events
FRC Magnolia Regional (Mississippi)
3/18 - 3/21
Created the first version of my Pit Collect website and put it to use.
FRC Championship
(Houston)
4/29 - 5/1
Started using API keys to grab standard information about teams, as well as more information and input sections
Mini Autopilot Panel
6/6
Vacuum Robot & Science Fair
7/1 - Present
Built a mini autopilot to control the autopilot in my flight simulator.
Built a mini autopilot to control the autopilot in my flight simulator.

FRC

2026 Robot

Created a type of scouting website called Pit Collect, which our team used to analyze the hardware and basic strategy of other teams
Can be used to figure out how to play against them
Determine how to cooperate with them when they are on the same side as us
Helped to build an advanced knowledge and understanding of HTML, JS, and CSS through the help of vibe coding and my own code.
Helped solder part of the wiring for the robot
Massively developed my soldering skills
Paved the way for future projects
Worked on object detection models for the 2026 robot
Helped to map out game pieces and compile into an object detection model for our robot
Taught me the basics of object detection and object detection software, such as Roboflow
Contributions

FRC Magnolia Regional
3/18 - 3/21

Results
12th out of 46 teams
Match record of 6-3-0.
Got into the semifinals of the playoff matches
Won the Impact Award
took us to the FRC Championship in Houston
My Pit Collect Website was used to track the data of over 40 teams.
Final Score: 
188:288

Struggles/Problems
To transfer data from the device the scouting was done on to the device used to compile all the results, we decided to use a qr code to transfer all the values

In the early stages of development, the QR code was too large, resulting in the scanner not being able to pick up the QR code
Solution:

When I was soldering wires, I sometimes used to accidentally burn the plastic/insulation of the wire and wire connectors, rendering the wires useless.
The soldering tin would not melt properly, and so I would keep the soldering iron on the component for a long time.
QR Code too large
Burned Wires
Solution:

QR Code Fix
To solve the issue of my QR code being too large, I utilized 4 main methods:
Setting Visual Dimension Limits
Set the QR code size to 256 by 256 px
Ensures the image size will not change
LZ-string Compression
Before any of the qr codes are generated, all the TSV(tab separated values) are compressed into Base64 format
E.g. A -> 000000, B -> 000001…
Character Sanitization
Newlines and tabs are deleted from text inputs to save space
Doesn’t this make the file size larger?
It does, but LZ string compression looks for recurring patterns and creates a dictionary for where the values should go
Back:

Soldering Skills Improvement
Since I kept the soldering iron on the component for too long, it caused the plastic surrounding the metal contacts to melt. This results in the component becoming unusable, which wastes time and resources.
Plug a spare connector in
By plugging in a spare connector, it acts as a heat sink. The extra metal contacts mean that more heat is required to raise the temperature of the component, allowing me to keep the soldering iron on for longer.
Pre-tin both the connector and the wire
I used to only pre-tin the wire, which meant that there will be poor heat transfer
By tinning the connector too, the metal heats up way quicker
Heat shrink wrap
XT-60 Connectors
Back:

FRC Houston Championships
4/29 - 5/1

Results
9 divisions in total
49th out of 75 teams in the Daly Division
My Pit collect website was used to scout over 70 international teams
Win loss record of 4-6-0
Added major features to my Pit Collect website
API key grabbing from the Blue Alliance to display basic information about a team.
Allowed for teams to draw out multiple autonomous strategies

Struggles/Problems
Robot wiring failures during match
During a lot of the matches, our robot could not move due to electrical wiring mistakes and zeroing issues due to human error
Time constraints
Autonomous path drawing is laggy
To lower the QR code size, I decided to lower the amount of points(x,y) that will be plotted when you drew on the field. 
This made the line drawing inaccurate and laggy, which meant we were compromising our data for file size
= lossy compression
Although I was not in the fixing team, this experience has taught me that even under pressure, you cannot skip steps in the standard procedure, and must follow the checklist as intended.

Johnson Space Center

Saturn V Rocket
When I visited the Johnson Space Center in Houston, the thing that stood out to me the most was the Saturn V Rocket. When I approached it, I was in awe of its massive size and complex engineering. 
Realization: True engineering requires everything to be done step by step, and everything has to be done to perfection. 

Space Shuttle Carrier
This modified Boeing 747 carrying the shuttle orbiter shows structural load distribution, as well as the aerodynamic modifications required for a B747 to transport the Space Shuttle Orbiter.
I examined the old flight controls and avionics, where I noticed that it still resembles modern flight displays today.
 

Johnson Space Center Reflections
Seeing how mechanical, electrical, and control systems come together in  Aerospace inspired me to build my own physical Flight Simulator Autopilot Panel. The large aircrafts and spacecrafts further inspired me to pursue the field of STEAM based majors.
Inspiration for Future Career
Further reinforced my goal to pursue EE/Mechanical Engineering/ Communications to become a pilot with a deep technical foundation in flight control systems

Flight Simulator Autopilot

Overview & Functionality
Physical autopilot hardware built to control heading, vertical speed, and navigation modes in flight simulation.
Integrates real-time rotary encoder inputs and LCD outputs to display live in-game flight data.

Software and Communication
Using Mobiflight, I created an instruction set that converts my inputs into in-game actions and also grabs live game data.
AP On/OFF
Vertical Speed
Heading Control/ VS Select
Altitude Controls
Display Modes
Navigation Modes

Hardware & Electrical
Primary Components:
Arduino Nano
6x6 mm buttons x11
Rotary Encoder w/ Push Button x2
LCD with I2C backpack
Jumper Wires
_____________________________________________

Daisy chained the Ground wire of each
 component to save space

Biggest Problem:
The soldering iron would often burn the 3d printed plastic, so I had to solder each component quickly before it melts the plastic
Example of daisy-chaining wires

Main Takeaways From this Project
My biggest takeaway from this project is the concept of daisy chaining wires. Instead of running individual, redundant ground wires to every single component, daisy chaining made the circuit design more efficient.
Impact: Reduced cable clutter, minimized signal clutter, and reduced the risk of short circuits.



Overcoming burnt insulation from my FRC soldering experiences taught me proper heat dissipation techniques and soldering techniques.
Learned to use spare connectors/conductive parts as heat sinks
Pre-tin both the wires and metal contacts
Use flux

AI Vacuum Robot: Overview & Current Progress
V1 Design

About
This project combines everything I have learned over the past few years about electronics, mechanical design, programming, and communications into one self-directed build. Unlike FRC, where I worked within a team and an existing robot platform, this vacuum robot is mine from spec to chassis to code: I am designing the mechanics, wiring the electronics, writing the AI object-detection pipeline, and documenting the entire process publicly on Instagram.

The Problem
Traditional robot vacuums rely solely on LIDAR or bump sensors. They can map walls accurately, but they blindly run over small, complex obstacles like charging cables, socks, or pet waste, causing damage to the robot or the home. A system that is only has map-based navigation has no concept of what an object actually is, only that something is or is not there.
???

The Solution
Computer Vision Integration: Runs a lightweight TensorFlow Lite machine learning model using a front-facing webcam.

Proactive Scanning: Scans the floor area ahead of time before the robot physically enters the space.

Low-Profile Hazard Detection: Identifies small, high-risk objects (like charging cables) that standard LIDAR or physical bump sensors usually miss or only react to after impact.

ROS Override: Temporarily overrides the ROS navigation stack to draw a dynamic "no-go" zone around the detected object for real-time path planning.


How the Vacuum Works: Suction + Brushing
Suction: A high-speed motor spins an impeller fan at roughly 30,000 RPM, creating a low-pressure zone inside the dustbin. Outside air rushes in to equalize that pressure, carrying dust and fine debris with it.
Active brushing (new): A dedicated brush motor now agitates dirt and hair directly off the floor as the primary cleaning force, with the impeller fan providing secondary suction to collect what the brush lifts, rather than relying on suction alone.
Why the change matters: Suction alone struggles with debris that is stuck to or embedded in carpet fibers. Mechanical agitation from a brush roller physically dislodges it first, which is how most commercial vacuums work, and is a lesson I learned by testing suction-only performance first.

System Architecture
High-Level Brain: Orange Pi 5 (8GB)
Runs ROS navigation and SLAM mapping
Runs the AI object-detection model
Upgraded from a Raspberry Pi 4 for more onboard compute headroom
Low-Level Controller: Arduino Mega
Receives velocity and motor commands from the Orange Pi
Converts commands into electrical pulses for the stepper and brush motors
Sensors
RPLIDAR C1 ~ 360-degree scanning for room mapping
Standard USB webcam ~ AI object detection (swapped from the Raspberry Pi Camera Module for easier integration with the Orange Pi)

Bill of Materials(Updated)
Computing & Control: Orange Pi 5 (8GB), Arduino Mega, iMax B6 charger/balancer
Sensors: RPLIDAR C1 (360-degree), USB webcam for AI object detection
Drivetrain: 2x NEMA 17 stepper motors, A4988 stepper drivers (unchanged), rubber wheels + front caster
Cleaning System (updated): Dedicated brush motor as the primary cleaning force, plus a DC motor + impeller fan for suction
Power: JFly 2200mAh battery, 5V/5A buck converter
Chassis: MDF or 3D-printed PETG base, DIY dustbin

Recent Fixes
Design pivot: from suction-only to active brushing.
Original design relied entirely on impeller suction, following the San Ace 40 fan approach from the first prototype.
Testing showed suction alone was inconsistent on embedded dirt and hair, matching the "weak suction" risk I had already flagged as an anticipated challenge in the design phase.
Solution: added a dedicated brush motor to physically agitate and lift debris, with suction not working alongside it rather than doing all the work alone. This mirrors how commercial vacuums combine agitation and suction.
Hardware swaps made during the build.
Raspberry Pi 4 to Orange Pi 5 (8GB) for more processing headroom for the AI model
Raspberry Pi Camera Module to a standard USB webcam for simpler wiring and driver support on the Orange Pi

Current Status
Phase: Hardware & Kinematics (Phase 1). Chassis is physically assembled and the drivetrain motors are mounted.
In progress: Wiring the electronics ~ connecting the Arduino Mega to the stepper drivers, brush motor, and power system before establishing basic remote-controlled movement.
Next steps: Bring up basic movement control, then move to Phase 2 ~ connecting the Orange Pi, configuring the ROS navigation stack, and getting the RPLIDAR C1 to generate a 2D map of a room.


Instagram Page
This is my Instagram Page that I will be using to document the process of my robot.

Why This Project: EE / ME / Communications
Building this robot end-to-end, mechanical design, electrical wiring, embedded control, and an AI vision pipeline, has shown me how much I enjoy work that sits between disciplines rather than inside just one. Solving the weak-suction problem was a mechanical engineering question; wiring the Arduino Mega to the stepper drivers was electrical; overriding the ROS navigation stack with the AI model was closer to computer engineering; and documenting the build publicly is its own communications challenge. This project has reinforced that I want a college major that lets me keep working across that boundary, rather than one that forces me to pick a single lane too early.

Science Fair
ADASB
